video_caption: The video opens with a computer screen displaying the OriginPro 8.64 software interface, featuring an open spreadsheet titled "Book1" on the left side, containing columns labeled "A(X)" and "B(Y)" and rows numbered 1 to 24, along with fields for "Long Name," "Units," and "Comments." The rest of the software window is a neutral grey. At the bottom of the screen, the taskbar shows two minimized window icons: "Chapter 3c X-Ray Diffraction -..." and "MIT_CrystalSizeAnalysis_Speak...". Around the 00:12 mark, the screen transitions to a white presentation slide with the bold black title "Crystallite Size Broadening." Below the title, a prominent formula is displayed: "B(2θ) = Kλ / L cosθ". Several bullet points explain the formula and related concepts, stating: "Peak Width due to crystallite size varies inversely with crystallite size," "as the crystallite size gets smaller, the peak gets broader," "The peak width varies with 2θ as cos θ," "The crystallite size broadening is most pronounced at large angles 2Theta," "However, the instrumental profile width and microstrain broadening are also largest at large angles 2theta," "peak intensity is usually weakest at larger angles 2Theta," "If using a single peak, often get better results from using diffraction peaks between 30 and 50 deg 2Theta," and "below 30deg 2Theta, peak asymmetry compromises profile analysis." The speaker is heard explaining the formula, referring to "Beta" as the full width at half maximum and "L" as the crystallite size. No people are visible throughout the segment.

The video segment displays a white presentation slide titled "Crystallite Size Broadening" in black font at the top. Below the title, a central equation is presented: "B(2θ) = Kλ / L cosθ". The rest of the slide contains bullet points explaining aspects of crystallite size broadening. The first main bullet states: "Peak Width due to crystallite size varies inversely with crystallite size," with a sub-point: "– as the crystallite size gets smaller, the peak gets broader." The second main bullet reads: "The peak width varies with 2θ as cos θ," followed by several sub-points: "– The crystallite size broadening is most pronounced at large angles 2Theta," "• However, the instrumental profile width and microstrain broadening are also largest at large angles 2theta," "• peak intensity is usually weakest at larger angles 2theta," and "– If using a single peak, often get better results from using diffraction peaks between 30 and 50 deg 2theta," with a final sub-point: "• below 30deg 2theta, peak asymmetry compromises profile analysis." A mouse cursor moves across the screen, highlighting different parts of the text as a male voice explains the Scherrer equation. The speaker identifies 'K' as a shape factor, 'λ' as the X-ray wavelength, 'L' as crystallite size, and 'θ' as the Bragg angle. He stresses that 'B(2θ)', the full width at half maximum (FWHM), must be used in radians, a common mistake where people mistakenly use degrees.

The video segment displays a white digital slide titled "Crystallite Size Broadening." Centered on the slide is an equation: "B(2θ) = Kλ / (L cos θ)." Below the equation, several bullet points elaborate on the concept. From 0:04 to 0:10, a hand-shaped cursor hovers over the "B(2θ)" term in the equation. The bullet points state: "Peak Width due to crystallite size varies inversely with crystallite size" (meaning, "as the crystallite size gets smaller, the peak gets broader"). The next main point is "The peak width varies with 2θ as cos θ," followed by sub-points explaining that "The crystallite size broadening is most pronounced at large angles 2Theta." However, it also notes that "the instrumental profile width and microstrain broadening are also largest at large angles 2Theta" and "peak intensity is usually weakest at larger angles 2Theta." A final sub-point advises, "If using a single peak, often get better results from using diffraction peaks between 30 and 50 deg 2theta" because "below 30deg 2theta, peak asymmetry compromises profile analysis."

The video opens with a slide titled "Crystallite Size Broadening," displaying the formula B(2θ) = Kλ / (L cosθ) and several bullet points explaining how peak width varies inversely with crystallite size, becoming broader as the crystallite size decreases. It also notes that peak width varies with 2θ as cos θ, making crystallite size broadening most pronounced at large 2Theta angles, although instrumental profile width and microstrain broadening are also largest there, and peak intensity is weakest. The text further advises using diffraction peaks between 30 and 50 degrees 2theta for single peak analysis, as asymmetry below 30 degrees 2theta compromises profile analysis. A cursor, represented by a human finger, points to the text, emphasizing the points about peak broadening and variation with 2θ. At 0:09, the screen transitions to a view of the OriginPro 9.0 64-bit software interface, which features a grey background with a smaller "Book1" worksheet open, showing numbered rows and columns A(X) and B(Y) with fields for Long Name, Units, and Comments. The speaker mentions that they will be using Origin and advises viewers to get a recent version, specifically noting that Origin versions less than 8 or 8.5 might not support the demonstrated function, while their current version is Origin 9.0. The cursor is then seen moving to highlight the "Analysis" menu option at the top of the software window.

The video segment opens with a computer screen displaying the OriginPro 9.0 64-bit software. On the left side, a spreadsheet-like window named "Book1" is visible, featuring columns labeled "A(X)" and "B(Y)" along with rows numbered 1 through 26. The rest of the OriginPro interface is a grey workspace. At 0:17, a Notepad window titled "alphafe2o3_900 - Notepad" appears, containing what appears to be X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The text includes various experimental parameters such as "Filename C:\Windmax\Data\alphafe2o3_900.raw", "Goniometer MiniFlex2 Goniometer +", "ScanningMode 2Theta/Theta", "X-Ray 30kV/15mA", "Start 10", "Stop 80", "Step 0.02", and "Offset 0". Below these parameters, a long list of numerical data is presented in two columns. The user then scrolls down and precisely selects all the numerical data in the Notepad file, from the first data point (10, 22.5) to the last (80, 5), indicated by a blue highlight. After copying the data, the Notepad window is minimized, and the user pastes the copied data directly into the "Book1" spreadsheet in OriginPro, starting from cell A1. The columns A(X) and B(Y) are populated with the numerical values, with column A containing the first set of numbers (likely 2-theta angles) and column B containing the second set (likely intensities). The populated columns are briefly highlighted in black before returning to their default appearance, showing the extensive dataset now loaded into OriginPro.

In the video segment, a user is demonstrating data plotting in OriginPro 9 64-bit software. A worksheet titled "Book1" is visible, displaying two columns of numerical data labeled "A(X)" and "B(Y)". The user has right-clicked on these selected columns, opening a context menu. The "Plot" option in this menu is highlighted in blue, indicating selection. This action further opens a sub-menu to the right, presenting various chart types. Within this sub-menu, "Line" is highlighted, leading to another sub-menu on the far right which displays different line styles. The "Line" option is again highlighted in this final sub-menu, preparing to generate a basic line plot from the selected data. The speaker's voice explains these steps: "Control and selected the two columns and right-clicked on them then went to plot and went to line then line."

The video demonstrates how to perform a Gaussian peak fit on a diffractogram using OriginPro software. It begins by showing a diffractogram (intensity vs. 2θ) with multiple peaks, then zooms into a single prominent peak around 33 degrees (0:04). The user navigates through the menu bar, selecting "Analysis" > "Peaks and Baseline" > "Multiple Peak Fit" > "Open Dialog..." (0:08-0:17). A dialog box appears, where "Gaussian" is chosen as the "Peak Function" (0:20-0:28). After clicking "OK", another dialog prompts the user to "Double click to pick peaks" (0:30). The user double-clicks on the peak, marking its center with a red line and displaying its X and Y coordinates (0:33-0:37). The user then clicks "Open NLFit" (NonLinear Fit), which opens the "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialog box, showing initial fit parameters like 'base', 'center', 'amplitude', and 'FWHM' (0:41-0:46). The graph now displays the raw data (purple) with a preliminary Gaussian fit (red curve) overlaid. The user clicks the "Fit until converged" button (0:53-0:57), causing the red fit curve to converge more closely to the experimental data. The "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialog box updates with the final parameter values, including the FWHM (w) of 0.19842 (0:57-1:02). The user then explores different tabs within the "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialog, showing the "Function Selection" (0:08-1:15), the "Fitting Function Formula" for Gaussian (0:15-1:20), and a "Sample Curve" diagram illustrating the Gaussian parameters (1:20-1:25). Finally, after clicking "Done" and confirming to switch to the report sheet, a comprehensive report is generated, displaying statistical data such as R-squared values, the equation used for fitting, and a summary of all fit parameters, including the FWHM, along with fitted curves and residual plots (1:45-2:02). The video briefly shows the raw fitted data points in a separate sheet (2:02-2:05) before returning to the graph with an overlaid table summarizing the fit results (2:05-2:28).

The video segment opens with a close-up on a scientific graph displaying a fluctuating purple line, labeled "B," and a smooth red curve, labeled "Gaussian Fit of Sheet1 B," representing a data fit. The x-axis is labeled "2θ" with values from 32 to 34, and a results table to the right shows the "Gaussian" model equation `y = y0 + A/ (w*sqrt(Pi/(4*ln(2)))) * exp(-4*ln(2)*((x-xc)/w)^2)`, a "Reduced Chi-Sqr" of 646.54243, and an "Adj. R-Square" of 0.37431, along with fitted parameter values for `y0`, `xc`, `A`, and `w`. A mouse cursor moves over the equation text. The view then zooms out, revealing the full graph with a y-axis labeled "Intensity" (0 to 400), and a vertical toolbar on the left. The mouse hovers over a magnifying glass icon, displaying a tooltip with "Scale Out" and "Restore axes scale" options. Subsequently, a "Project Explorer" panel appears on the left, listing "UNTITLED" (project), "Folder1," and items like "Book1" (currently selected), "Graph1," and "Table1," while the graph and results table remain visible on the right side of the screen.

The video demonstrates how to perform a multiple Gaussian peak fit on a graph using OriginLab software. It begins by showing a results window with "Summary" and "ANOVA" tables, along with small preview plots. The scene then shifts to a spreadsheet named "Sheet1" containing two columns of data, "A(X)" and "B(Y)". The user creates a line graph from this data by navigating through the "Plot" menu. A new graph, labeled "Graph2," appears with "Intensity" on the Y-axis and unnamed units on the X-axis, displaying a series of sharp purple peaks. A "Reminder Message" dialog briefly appears explaining that "Origin graphs are created from templates" and "A System Theme is by default applied," which the user dismisses by clicking "OK". The user then zooms into a specific section of the graph containing three prominent peaks using a magnifying glass tool to draw a selection box. Next, the user accesses the "Analysis" menu, hovers over "Peaks and Baseline," and selects "Multiple Peak Fit" to open a dialog. In the "Spectroscopy: nlfitpeaks" dialog, "Gaussian" is selected as the "Peak Function," and the user clicks "OK". A "Get Points" dialog prompts the user to "Double click to pick peaks." The user proceeds to double-click on the apex of each of the three visible peaks. As each peak is picked, a red vertical line with a horizontal marker appears, and the "Get Points" dialog updates, confirming "You have picked 1 peaks," then "2 peaks," and finally "3 peaks," along with their X and Y coordinates. After picking all three, the "Open NLFit" button is clicked. This action opens the "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialog box, which overlays the graph. On the graph, the original purple peaks are now accompanied by fitted blue Gaussian curves. The "NLFit" dialog displays a table of parameters for each peak (y0, xc, A, w for center, amplitude, and FWHM, respectively) and a "Messages" tab showing "(1) Parameter Initialization was called." The user then clicks the "Fit" button, and the "Messages" tab begins to display "Iterating..." messages, indicating the fitting process is underway.

The video demonstrates a peak fitting process on a graphical display of X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. Initially, the screen shows a graph with two prominent peaks, numerically labeled '1' and '2', along with a smaller third peak. A dialogue box titled "Auto Parameter Initialization" is open, displaying a table of parameters like "base," "center," "amplitude," and "FWHM" for multiple peaks. Below the table, a "Messages" tab indicates that "Parameter Initialization was called," followed by a series of increasing iteration numbers, suggesting an ongoing fitting process. The user then interrupts this process, and a message "Fit aborted - user has cancelled the iterations" appears, explaining that the fitting algorithm failed to capture the third peak effectively due to its small size. Following this, the graph is zoomed out to reveal a broader range of XRD peaks. The user then accesses the "Analysis" menu, selecting "Peaks and Baseline" and "Multiple Peak Fit" to open a new fitting dialogue. In this "Spectroscopy: nlfitpeaks" window, the user chooses "Gaussian" as the peak function and clicks "OK." A smaller "Get Points" window instructs the user to double-click to pick peaks. The user then precisely clicks on the two most intense peaks on the graph. The main "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialogue box reappears, now pre-filled with parameters for these two selected peaks. The user initiates the fit, and the "Messages" tab confirms that the "Fit converged" after "12" iterations, indicating a successful fitting of the two prominent peaks.

The video segment details the process and results of fitting Gaussian peaks to data within a software interface. It opens with an "NLFit (Gaussian)" dialog box displaying various parameters (y0, xc, A, w for two peaks) with their values, standard errors, and fit settings. The user clicks "Done" (00:05). A graph then appears, showing experimental data (purple line labeled "B") with two distinct peaks, along with individual Gaussian fits for each peak ("Fit Peak 1" in red, "Fit Peak 2" in green) and a cumulative fit (blue line labeled "Cumulative Fit Peak") which closely matches the experimental data (00:06). A "Reminder Message" dialog box pops up asking, "Do you want to switch to the report sheet?", to which the user selects "Yes, and do the same in the future, no need to ask again." and clicks "OK" (00:11-00:13). The screen transitions to a detailed report sheet titled "Nonlinear Curve Fit (Gaussian) (10-09-2017 16:31:50)", presenting tables of fit parameters, equations, and statistics like "Reduced Chi-Sqr" (445.16713) and "Adj. R-Square" (0.56919) (00:14). On the left, a "Project Explorer" shows project files; the user clicks "Graph2" (00:16). The view switches back to the graph, now with a floating table containing the Gaussian model equation and fit parameters (y0, xc, A, w values) overlaid. This table is then dragged to the right side of the graph (00:17-00:23). The video highlights the "w" (Full Width at Half Maximum) values for the two peaks: 0.19914 for Peak 1 and 0.21746 for Peak 2 (00:24-00:28), concluding with the graph and parameter table remaining on screen (00:30).

The video segment opens with a scientific data display featuring a 2D plot and a table of fitting parameters. The plot, labeled with "2Θ" on the x-axis and intensity values on the y-axis, shows a purple data curve labeled "B" with two distinct peaks. Overlaid are three fitted curves: a red line for "Fit Peak 1," a green line for "Fit Peak 2," and a blue line for "Cumulative Fit Peak." To the right, a table presents the "Gaussian" model equation ("y = y0 + A/(w*sqrt(Pi/(4*ln(2)))) * exp(-4*ln(2)*((x-xc)/w)^2)"), its "Reduced Chi-Sqr" (445.16713), and "Adj. R-Square" (0.55919). Below this, fitting parameters for "Peak1(B)" (y0: 14.89832, xc: 33.23317, A: 90.64318, w: 0.19914) and "Peak2(B)" (y0: 14.89832, xc: 35.68706, A: 68.12661, w: 0.21746) are listed with their respective "Value." A white mouse cursor is visible in the top right corner. The scene then transitions at 0:11 to an outro screen with a light brown, geometric-patterned background. A silver laptop on the left displays a landscape image of green hills, blue sky, and white clouds, with a blue arrow pointing from the screen to the text "More Videos" in a handwritten-style font. On the right, three social media icons (Facebook, Twitter, and Google+) are stacked vertically. At 0:24, a red rectangular button with the text "subscribe" slides into view from the right side of the screen.
